**Tier 4** — decisions — policies, overrides, scenarios · owned by `policy-ui` · `public.disruption_scenarios`

**One row is** One disruption applied to one node of one project: a capacity cut, a delay, or both. The ORIGINAL disruption shape, superseded in design by the `disruption_scenario_*` profile/target/effect/setting split but never migrated — both are live and neither reads the other.

TWO DISRUPTION MODELS ARE LIVE AT ONCE AND NEITHER READS THE OTHER. This table is the 2025-08-26 shape — one row per node, capacity and delay inline. The `disruption_scenario_profiles`/`_targets`/`_effects`/`_settings` group is the 2025-08-27 redesign that normalises the same idea. Nothing migrated the rows and nothing deprecates either, so a project can hold disruptions in both and a reader of one sees half the picture. Naming that is this sidecar's job; deciding it is not, and it belongs with WP 6.4's gap check.

Audited from WP 6.4: the three statement-grain triggers land with this sidecar, because `dataPlaneAudit.test.ts` scopes its rule to tables IN the contract and a deferred table's writes are unaudited with nothing to notice (D54).

`CSV header` is the name the **user types**, which is not always the column name —
that gap is defect D21. A dash means the column has no CSV origin.

| Column | CSV header | Type | Unit | Required in CSV | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `id` 🔑 | — | `uuid` | — | — | Surrogate key. The natural key is below; this is what the child rows reference. |
| `project_id` | — | `uuid` | — | — | The project this row belongs to. |
| `plant_name` | — | `text` | — | — | The plant this scenario belongs to, by display name. A project has one plant_name, so this is a denormalised copy of `projects.plant_name` rather than a second identity. |
| `node_id` | — | `text` | — | — | The node the disruption is applied to, by its display id — the same string the network pages use. Not a uuid and not a foreign key: a scenario may name a node that no longer exists in the graph, and deleting it silently would lose the decision. |
| `scenario_name` | — | `text` | — | — | What the person called this scenario. Not unique — see `natural_key_unique` below, which is the surrogate id and nothing else. |
| `capacity_reduction_percent` | — | `numeric` | `percent` | — | How much of the node's capacity the scenario removes. A PERCENT, not a fraction: the column name says so and the default of 0 means 'no reduction'. |
| `time_delay_days` | — | `numeric` | `days` | — | Additional delay the scenario imposes at this node. DAYS, and it is NOT normalised at promotion the way a tier-2 lead time is — this is a decision the user typed, not an observation, so it is stored as entered and converted where it is read. |
| `description` | — | `text` | — | — | Free text the person wrote. Never parsed. |
| `created_by` | — | `uuid` | — | — | The user who created the row, as a uuid. Client-asserted — this application authenticates against `approved_users` rather than Supabase Auth (D28) — so it names who the client said acted, which is why the audit row added by WP 6.4 is the record that matters. |
| `organization` | — | `text` | — | — | The tenant's DISPLAY NAME, carried on every row of this vintage. `uuid- identity` (G1) says a displayable name is never a join key: nothing joins on this, and `organization_id` is the identity. Kept because the rows exist. |
| `created_at` | — | `timestamp with time zone` | — | — | When the row was created. Server-stamped, never the client's clock. |
| `updated_at` | — | `timestamp with time zone` | — | — | When it was last changed. Server-stamped by the `update_*_updated_at` trigger. |
| `sim_payload` | — | `jsonb` | — | — | The scenario as the simulator receives it, frozen at save time. A denormalised copy of the columns above plus whatever the caller added; nothing reads it back into the columns, so a divergence between the two is possible and unnoticed. |
| `from_network` | — | `boolean` | — | — | Whether the scenario was created by clicking a node on a network page (true) or entered by hand. Defaults true, so a row written by any other path claims a provenance it may not have. |

> Reaches no engine field. `project_map.py` builds the engine's world from the tier-2 tables and the policy bundle; a disruption is applied by the SIMULATOR at run time from `sim_payload`, not by the mapper from this column. So the value a person types here is read by the scenario runner and by nothing the data contract traces (§5 T1: the number has a source, and that source is this row).

### `time_delay_days`

Additional delay the scenario imposes at this node. DAYS, and it is NOT normalised at promotion the way a tier-2 lead time is — this is a decision the user typed, not an observation, so it is stored as entered and converted where it is read.

| | |
|---|---|
| Type | `numeric`, default `0` |
| Grain | `level` |
| Unit | `days` — fixed |
| Added by | `20250826180749_e9181074-55e6-4724-98c3-3c4b648aa891.sql` |
| Read by the engine | **not traced** |
| Validated at ingest | — |
| Rendered at | *not yet recorded (WP 5.1)* |

> Reaches no engine field, for the same reason as `capacity_reduction_percent`. Note the unit is in the COLUMN NAME rather than in a unit column — the opposite of the tier-2 convention `lead_time`/`lead_time_unit` that `normalize-at-promotion` (I3) governs. That is defensible for a decision (there is one unit and it cannot vary) and it is worth stating, because a reader who has learned the tier-2 rule will look for the companion column.
